articles.title: Your RAG answer is wrong: retrieval or the model?
articles.dek: A three-minute test that tells you which half of a retrieval system failed, before anyone changes a prompt or swaps a model.

body.text: A team ships a documentation assistant. In week one it answers a question about the refund window with a figure nobody recognises. The fix that gets tried first is almost always the same: a stronger model, then a longer prompt, then a plea to the vendor. Weeks go by. The answer stays wrong.

The uncomfortable part is that none of those steps were diagnostic. They were guesses about which half of the system failed, made without looking. And a retrieval system only has two halves worth separating: what got fetched, and what the model did with it.
Look at the retrieved text before you touch the prompt.
The three-minute test

items: Take the failing question and log the exact chunks that were retrieved for it, in the order they were passed.
Read them yourself. Does the correct answer appear anywhere in that text, in plain words?
If it does not appear, the retrieval half failed and no prompt will fix it.

If it does appear, paste the same chunks into a fresh chat with the same question. If the model now answers correctly, your assembly is at fault: order, truncation or a conflicting instruction. If it still answers wrongly, the model half failed.
Write down which half it was, next to the question, and keep the note. Five of those notes is a pattern.

body.text: Most teams who run this honestly for a week find the split lands somewhere near two thirds retrieval, one third everything else. That is not a law of nature, but it is common enough to be worth expecting: the model is usually doing a reasonable job on text that never should have been handed to it.
What each half actually breaks on

rows: Retrieval
The right passage was never fetched
Chunk size, the index's freshness, and whether the query is embedded the same way as the documents
Retrieval
The right passage was fetched and then cut off
Token budget and truncation order: the useful chunk is often last
Assembly
The passage is present but contradicted
A system prompt, an older summary, or a memory note that disagrees with it
Model
The passage is present, clear, and ignored
Instruction conflict, or asking for a format the content cannot fill
Model
The passage is absent and an answer appears anyway
No instruction to decline, and no check that the claim is grounded

body.text: The decision this leads to

Once you know which half fails, the engineering choice is no longer a matter of taste. A retrieval failure is a data and indexing problem: reindex on a schedule, chunk on headings rather than character counts, and store the document date so stale text can be filtered out instead of out-argued. A model failure is a design problem: supply the fact rather than ask for it, require a quotation from the source, and allow the answer “not in the documents” to be a success rather than a defect.

There is also a third outcome worth naming. Sometimes the retrieved text is correct, the model's answer is correct, and the user still calls it wrong — because the document itself is out of date. That is not an AI failure at all. It is a content problem that the assistant has made visible, and the honest response is to fix the document.
Try this week

items: Pick the three complaints you have heard most about your assistant and run the three-minute test on each.
Log the retrieved chunks for every answer from now on. A system you cannot inspect is a system you can only guess about.
Add one test to your evaluation set per confirmed failure, with the question and the answer you expect, so the next change has to keep passing it.

body.text: The point is not the test itself. It is the habit of naming the failing part before changing anything — the same habit the ExplAIn course builds across all eight parts of an AI system, starting with the map in Module 01.

articles.takeaway: Read the retrieved text before you blame the model: if the answer was never fetched, no prompt can save it.

articles.title: Most of what you call the AI is not the model
articles.dek: A map of the eight parts around the model, and a five-minute method for drawing it for any product.

body.text: A support assistant starts quoting refund terms that changed three months ago. The team swaps in a newer model. Same wrong terms. Someone rewrites the prompt. Still wrong. Two weeks later a developer notices the policy document in the search index was never reindexed. The model was never the problem.

This happens because the word “AI” gets used for the whole product. When something breaks, there is nowhere to point except the model, so that is what gets replaced. A map fixes that. Once you can name the parts, you can name which part failed.

The model is narrow: weights behind an endpoint. Text in, predicted text out. No memory between calls. No access to your data. No ability to do anything unless something else runs the action. Everything else a user experiences was built by people, on purpose.
The model generates. The system does.
Four boxes that feed the model

rows: Context
Everything assembled into this one call: instructions, history, retrieved text
Knowledge
Facts the model never trained on: your documents, your data, today’s prices
Memory and state
What survives between calls, and what a half-finished run carries forward
Interface
What a user can ask, what they see, and how a wrong answer looks to them

body.text: Four boxes that decide what happens

rows: Tools and actions
Which real systems it can read, and which ones it can change
Orchestration
Which steps run, in what order, and whether code or the model chose
Guardrails
Permissions, filters, limits and approvals wrapped around the model
Evaluation
The repeatable tests that tell you the product got better or worse

body.text: Cost and latency are not a ninth box. Every box adds some. A retrieval step, a second model call, a validation pass, an approval queue: each one buys you something and charges you for it on every request. That trade is easier to argue about when the boxes have names.
Map any product in five minutes

items: Pick one real user request and trace it from the interface to the answer, step by step.
Mark the model call. Every other step on the list belongs to the system.
Sort each step into the eight boxes. One step can touch two of them.
For each empty box ask: missing by design, or missing because nobody decided?
Circle the box most likely to fail first, and name the person who owns it.

body.text: Do this on a whiteboard with the people who built the thing. The argument is the point. Most teams discover that two of them believed different things about what is actually sent to the model on each request.

The most common empty box is evaluation. Products ship on the strength of one good demo, and nobody can say whether last week’s prompt change helped. An empty box is not always a bug, but an unnoticed empty box usually is.
ExplAIn is built on this map. The first module draws it, and every module after that goes deep into one box: context, knowledge and memory, tools, orchestration, guardrails and evaluation.

articles.takeaway: Name the box before you fix anything, and rule out context, knowledge and tools before you blame the model.

articles.title: Why a confident answer is not a verified one
articles.dek: How fluent text goes wrong, what confidence actually measures, and which outputs a product must check in code.

body.text: A billing assistant tells a customer their late fee is $34.50. The number is wrong. Nothing in the reply looks wrong: the sentence is well formed, the tone is calm, the format matches every correct answer the assistant has ever produced. That is the whole problem in one screenshot.

Ask a model the same question three times and you may get three different answers in the same steady voice. The voice never wavers, because the voice is generated the same way the facts are. It is output, not a report on the output.

The mechanism explains it. At each step the model scores the possible next tokens, settings reshape those scores, one token is sampled, and the pick joins the context for the next step. An early wrong detail is therefore not corrected. It becomes the ground the rest of the answer stands on.
Confidence is not correctness.
What confidence is and is not

items: A hedge or a firm tone is generated text. It is not a measurement of whether the claim is true.
Token probabilities are a real signal about the text, not a truth score for the claim it makes.
Low temperature narrows variety, not error. If the top token is wrong, it is wrong consistently.
More reasoning improves math, code and planning. It cannot supply a fact nobody gave the model.
Asking “are you sure?” produces another sample from the same model, drawn from the same gaps.

body.text: Fabrication clusters where the training text was thin and the pressure to answer is high: rare facts, exact figures, dates, identifiers, citations. A model trained to be helpful will usually produce something rather than decline. Fluent filler is the most likely continuation, so fluent filler is what you get.
Where a product must verify, not trust

columns: How to check without the model
rows: A number, price, date or ID
Fetch it from the system of record and let the model only phrase it
Structured data going into code
Validate the schema and the values, then reject, retry or fall back
A citation or a source link
Resolve the reference; if it does not resolve, drop the claim
Generated code
Compile it and run the tests; a passing suite is not an opinion
Quality after any change
Rerun a fixed test set, because one good demo is one sample

body.text: Notice what these have in common: none of them ask the model to grade itself. A check is only a check if it can disagree with the thing it is checking, which means it has to come from code, data, a rule or a person.
Deciding output by output

items: If variety is the point, such as names and first drafts, leave it probabilistic and test with real users.
If a person reads it beside the source, probabilistic is fine. Show the source next to it.
If code consumes it, validate structure and values before anything downstream sees it.
If it states a number, price, date or citation, look the value up instead of generating it.
If it moves money or triggers an action, code computes and permits it, and a person approves the risky ones.

body.text: One warning about the easy answer. “A human reviews it” only counts if that person has the time, the tooling and a realistic volume. A reviewer who approves four hundred items a day is a rubber stamp with a job title, and everyone involved knows it.
ExplAIn spends a module on this mechanism and a later one on the checks: what to verify, where the check lives in your system, and how to test that it still works after a model or prompt change.

articles.takeaway: Treat every output as a likely guess until something outside the model checks it.

articles.title: Autonomy is a cost, so decide where you spend it
articles.dek: How to choose between a fixed workflow, one model-chosen branch and a full agent loop, and where approval belongs.

body.text: A team is asked to make the weekly sales report “agentic.” The steps have not changed in two years: three queries, a chart, a paragraph of narrative, sent on Monday. The agent version makes eleven model calls, costs far more, and sometimes reorders the sections. The engineering was fine. Nobody asked the design question.

That question cuts through every agent pitch and roadmap slide: who decides the next step, your code or the model? That is all an agent is. A loop where the model picks the next action from what it has seen. It observes the goal and the last result, decides, your system runs the action and records it, then checks the limits.
Autonomy is a cost. Pay it only where fixed code can’t cover the cases.
A spectrum, not a switch

rows: Single call
Your code. One model call fills in one step
Fixed chain
Your code, in an order you wrote down
Router
The model picks one branch, then fixed code runs
Bounded agent
The model, inside step, budget and time limits
Autonomous agent
The model, including the decision to stop

body.text: Count the decisions the model makes, not the number of model calls. A pipeline with six calls in a fixed order is still a workflow. And note that the model never acts: it requests, your code executes. A plan is text it wrote and reads back, so nothing holds it to that plan unless you build something that does.
Why a chain of good steps still fails

items: A misread result enters state, and every later step treats it as an established fact.
An early wrong plan keeps steering the run even as the results disagree with it.
A failing action gets retried without progress until some limit finally stops it.
An email sent or a record deleted stays wrong after you fix the underlying bug.

body.text: The arithmetic is unforgiving, and worth doing on the back of an envelope. Take steps that each succeed nine times in ten, where one miss ruins the run, and ten of them in a row finish clean about a third of the time. The number is illustrative. The shape is the lesson: fewer uncontrolled steps beats a better model.
Where human approval belongs

rows: Read, search, summarize, draft
Runs automatically, with the output shown before use
Reversible changes: labels, notes
Automatic, logged, and genuinely easy to undo
Anything a customer receives
A person approves, at least until you have measured it
Money, deletion, permissions
Always approved, or never exposed as a tool at all

body.text: Approval follows risk and reversibility, and it has a budget. Every low-stakes confirmation you add spends attention that the high-stakes one will need. Approve few things, show the evidence and the exact diff, and make saying no as easy as saying yes.

items: If every input takes the same steps, write a workflow and let the model fill in steps.
If inputs fall into a few known paths, use a router: one model decision, then fixed code.
If the path depends on what it finds and the tools are read-only, use a bounded agent with caps.
If you cannot yet measure whole runs, stay one level less autonomous until you can.

body.text: ExplAIn has a module on this: the loop, the spectrum, how errors compound, and how to redesign a real use case at three levels of autonomy so the trade-offs are on the table before anyone builds.

articles.takeaway: Give the model a decision only where fixed code can’t handle the variety, and keep a person on anything you can’t undo.
